items.locator: Post-anaphylaxis monitoring: symptoms can resolve and later return as a biphasic reaction; emergency evaluation/monitoring is appropriate after treatment and observation is individualized according to the reaction and clinical course.
items.stem: After treatment for anaphylaxis, a client's symptoms have completely resolved. Why may continued observation still be appropriate?

options.A: A biphasic reaction can recur after initial resolution.
options.B: Every client develops a second reaction at the same fixed time.
options.C: Recurrence can occur only after another allergen exposure.
options.D: Residual epinephrine commonly causes a second anaphylactic episode.

items.rationale: Anaphylaxis can recur after apparent initial resolution as a biphasic reaction, so continued observation may be appropriate based on severity, treatment needs, and risk factors. Option A is correct. Biphasic reactions are not inevitable or predictably timed, do not require a new exposure, and are not caused by residual epinephrine.
items.finding: Fresh audit removed any fixed observation-hour claim and retained current risk-based monitoring to avoid overgeneralization.

items.locator: Heat Stroke section: very high body temperature with central nervous system dysfunction such as confusion, altered mental status or loss of consciousness is a medical emergency requiring emergency services and rapid cooling.
items.version: CDC/NIOSH Heat-related Illnesses page updated 2026-03-03; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A client exercising in extreme heat has a core temperature of 40.5°C (104.9°F) and confusion. Which condition should the nurse suspect?

options.D: A normal response to strenuous exercise.

items.rationale: Very high core temperature accompanied by central nervous system dysfunction such as confusion is characteristic of heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency requiring rapid cooling and emergency care. Option B is correct. Heat exhaustion and uncomplicated dehydration do not account for this severe hyperthermia with altered mental status.
items.finding: Fresh audit removed padded alternatives and kept the two defining heat-stroke discriminators in the stem.

items.locator: Moderate hypothermia/management: temperatures about 28-32°C are moderate; handle patients gently because of dysrhythmia risk, prevent further heat loss, use active external rewarming for moderate hypothermia with heat directed to the trunk, and monitor cardiac status.
items.stem: A client exposed to cold has a core temperature of 31°C (87.8°F), confusion, and slowed responses. Which management principle is most appropriate?

options.A: Encourage vigorous walking to rewarm quickly.
options.B: Handle gently, prevent further heat loss, actively rewarm the trunk, and monitor cardiac rhythm.
options.C: Massage the arms and legs vigorously.
options.D: Use unmonitored direct high heat on numb skin.

items.rationale: A core temperature of 31°C with altered mental status is clinically significant hypothermia. Care includes gentle handling, prevention of further heat loss, active external rewarming focused on the trunk, and cardiac monitoring because dysrhythmias can occur. Option B is correct. Vigorous exercise, extremity massage, and uncontrolled direct heat are unsafe.
items.finding: Fresh audit removed the outdated 'rewarm slowly to prevent rewarming shock' concept and aligned management with current hypothermia guidance.

items.source_name: Wilderness Medical Society — Frostbite Clinical Practice Guideline Summary 2024
items.locator: Field/clinical rewarming: when thawing can be maintained and refreezing prevented, rapidly rewarm frostbite in circulating water at 37-39°C; avoid rubbing/massage and direct dry heat, and protect thawed tissue from refreezing and trauma.
items.version: WMS Frostbite Clinical Practice Guideline Summary 2024; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A client with frostbitten fingers arrives where refreezing can be prevented. Which rewarming method is appropriate?

options.A: Rapidly rewarm the fingers in circulating water at about 37-39°C.
options.B: Massage the frozen fingers vigorously while warming.
options.C: Apply a heating pad directly to numb tissue.
options.D: Let the fingers thaw slowly at room temperature despite a controlled warm-water bath.

items.rationale: WMS recommends rapid water-bath rewarming at 37-39°C when thawing can be maintained and refreezing prevented. Option A is correct. Rubbing and direct dry heat can worsen tissue injury, while slow room-temperature thawing is inferior when controlled rapid rewarming is available.
items.finding: Fresh audit retained the current 2024 WMS temperature range and removed answer-explaining padding.

items.source_name: American Red Cross — Debunking Dry or Delayed/Secondary Drowning
items.locator: Nonfatal drowning follow-up: obsolete terms such as dry/secondary/delayed drowning are not accepted diagnoses; a person with respiratory symptoms after a drowning event who becomes normal may be observed for several hours, and deterioration occurs with preceding respiratory symptoms rather than sudden unexpected death days later after complete recovery.
items.version: American Red Cross guidance dated 2024-08-12; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: An adult had coughing and brief breathing difficulty after a drowning event but is now alert with normal breathing and oxygenation in the emergency department. Which statement is most accurate?

options.A: A symptom-free client can suddenly die from 'secondary drowning' several days later without warning.
options.B: Observation for several hours is appropriate; discharge may be considered if the client remains completely normal.
options.C: No emergency evaluation is useful once spontaneous breathing returns.
options.D: Any respiratory symptom days later must automatically be attributed to delayed drowning.

items.rationale: Terms such as 'secondary' or 'dry' drowning are not accepted diagnoses. After a true nonfatal drowning with respiratory symptoms, observation for several hours is appropriate, and discharge may be reasonable if the person remains completely normal. Option B is correct. A and D perpetuate obsolete delayed-drowning myths, while C dismisses appropriate assessment after respiratory impairment.
items.finding: Fresh audit clarified that the client actually experienced respiratory impairment, preventing confusion between a drowning event and an asymptomatic water incident.

items.source_name: Mayo Clinic Laboratories — Amikacin, Random, Serum (ordering guidance for peak/trough testing)
items.locator: Ordering Guidance: a trough specimen should be collected immediately before the next scheduled dose; a peak specimen is collected 30-60 minutes after the last dose.
items.version: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories test catalog entry RAMIK/37033; live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A provider orders an amikacin trough concentration. When should the specimen be collected?

options.A: Immediately after the dose is given.
options.C: Immediately before the next scheduled dose.
options.D: Only after amikacin has been permanently discontinued.

items.rationale: Mayo Clinic Laboratories directs that an amikacin trough specimen be collected immediately before the next scheduled dose. Option C is correct. Immediately after dosing is closer to a peak context, random midpoint timing is not a trough, and testing is performed during therapy rather than only after discontinuation.
items.finding: Fresh audit corrected the laboratory-source hierarchy from a general nursing text to Mayo Clinic Laboratories and narrowed the generic trough question to a specific monitored drug.

items.source_name: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS — Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report
items.locator: DKA diagnostic assessment: DKA is characterized by diabetes/hyperglycemia, elevated ketones and metabolic acidosis; direct beta-hydroxybutyrate measurement is preferred when available, and the anion gap should not be used alone as a resolution criterion.
items.version: 2024 international consensus report, Diabetes Care 47(8):1257-1275; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A client with diabetes has hyperglycemia, elevated ketones, metabolic acidosis, and an increased anion gap. How should the nurse interpret the increased anion gap?

options.A: It supports high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis from accumulated unmeasured acids such as ketoacids.
options.C: It proves a primary respiratory acidosis.
options.D: It independently proves that diabetic ketoacidosis has resolved.

items.rationale: An increased anion gap supports high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis caused by unmeasured acids such as ketoacids. Option A is correct. It does not indicate alkalosis or prove a respiratory disorder, and current DKA guidance cautions against using the anion gap alone as a resolution criterion.
items.finding: Fresh audit preserved the important limitation that the anion gap is supportive rather than a stand-alone DKA resolution marker.

items.source_name: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS — Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report
items.locator: HHS diagnostic criteria/clinical presentation: severe hyperglycemia (typically glucose >=600 mg/dL), hyperosmolality, and profound dehydration with minimal significant ketoacidosis; cognitive changes can accompany marked hyperosmolality.
items.version: 2024 international consensus report, Diabetes Care 47(8):1257-1275; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A dehydrated client has a glucose level of 650 mg/dL, markedly elevated effective serum osmolality, and altered mental status. Which condition is most consistent with this pattern?
items.rationale: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state is characterized by severe hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and profound dehydration from osmotic diuresis, often with neurologic changes. Option B is correct. The measured glucose and hyperosmolality exclude hypoglycemia and water intoxication, and fasting ketosis does not produce this extreme hyperglycemic hyperosmolar picture.
items.finding: Fresh audit removed padded distractors and aligned the blueprint with diagnostic/laboratory interpretation under Reduction of Risk Potential.

items.source_name: American College of Cardiology — 2020 ACC/AHA Valvular Heart Disease Guideline: Key Perspectives, Part 3
items.locator: Prosthetic-valve antithrombotic therapy: mechanical mitral valve replacement requires vitamin K antagonist anticoagulation with a target INR of 3.0; targets differ for mechanical aortic valves/risk profiles.
items.version: 2020 ACC/AHA Valvular Heart Disease guideline remains the current ACC/AHA valve guideline in 2026; next major update is anticipated in 2027; currentness live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A client with a mechanical mitral valve replacement is receiving warfarin. What target INR is recommended by the ACC/AHA valve guideline?

options.D: No INR target because a direct oral anticoagulant is preferred.

items.rationale: ACC/AHA guidance specifies a target INR of 3.0 for a mechanical mitral valve replacement. Option B is correct. Other mechanical valves may have different targets, which is why the stem specifies the mitral position. Direct oral anticoagulants are not substituted for vitamin K antagonist therapy in this setting.
items.finding: Fresh audit confirmed the 2020 guideline remains current in 2026, preserved the valve-position qualifier, and removed rationale-padding from the numeric choices.

items.source_name: Mayo Clinic Laboratories — Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN), Serum
items.locator: Clinical Information/Interpretation: BUN may rise in prerenal states including water depletion and reduced renal perfusion/cardiac decompensation; BUN and creatinine are interpreted together with the clinical picture and other data.
items.version: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories BUN test catalog entry 81793; live-rechecked 2026-08-15.
items.stem: A client with vomiting and poor intake is clinically volume depleted and has an elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: The elevation can be consistent with a prerenal process related to water depletion or reduced renal perfusion.
options.B: The finding proves a postrenal obstruction.
options.C: The finding demonstrates improved glomerular filtration.
options.D: BUN is unrelated to hydration or renal perfusion.

items.rationale: BUN can increase in prerenal states such as water depletion and reduced renal perfusion. Option A appropriately interprets the result in the clinical context without treating BUN as diagnostic by itself. B overstates specificity, C reverses the meaning, and D is false.
items.finding: Fresh audit corrected the laboratory-source hierarchy to Mayo Clinic Laboratories and removed a potentially overgeneralized BUN:creatinine ratio threshold from the item.
